notes: A quiet aftermath with no fork left to take: the player walks the stairs they climbed twice and watches who leaves and how, the tells showing in where boxes sit and what is said on landings. The scene ends when the housekeeper locks the study with the new master's key.
opening: The thaw has come overnight and the house drips from every gutter; the drive is black slush and the first cart stands at the kitchen door. On the stair head Major Carrington buttons his coat with your rounds book, the stub and the study key in his breast pocket, Mr Ellingham beside him saying which of it will stand before a magistrate. Mr Yardley, master since the reading of the will, has pressed a second key into your hand and gone to wait at the study end, and below you Mr Fairbrother is carrying forty years down the back stairs in one box, the lid tied with cord. Lavinia Netherby comes behind him with hers.

variants.text: Miss Gresham comes down past you with her chin up and her gloves on, the ring no longer on her hand. She does not look at Mr Yardley and she says nothing to the solicitor of why. Grey snow light through the half-landing window; the barometer has begun, at last, to climb.

Miss Gresham stops at the newel post beside Mr Ellingham and speaks low, and you catch 'the housekeeper's drawer' before she sees you and finishes the sentence anyway. The barometer has begun to climb. The snow light is the same grey it has been for three days.
Meltwater ticks past the half-landing window. The barometer needle has moved for the first time in three days. The Major's gloves lie on the newel post, waiting for his hands.
Mrs Ormsby comes along the Turkey runner on the doctor's arm, slow, and passes the Major's man at the sconce without a word or a glance. The widow's door stands open behind her on a stripped bed.

Mrs Ormsby pauses on the doctor's arm by the Major's man and says, as if of the weather, 'The housekeeper's apron was very full that night, I thought,' and goes on. The widow's door stands open behind her on a stripped bed.
The sconces are out. The case of waxwings has been turned to the wall by someone packing. Three doors stand open on three stripped beds.

The tallow box is squared on its shelf, its lid down, its edge exactly to the edge of the board, the way it was kept for forty years. Mr Fairbrother's box stands by the baize door with its cord tied in a valet's knot.

The tallow box lies where you left it, lid askew, a stub rolled against the pail hook. Mr Fairbrother has looked at it and left it. His own box stands by the baize door with its cord tied in a valet's knot.
The smoke mark above the shelf is the only thing here that has not been packed or carried. Through the baize door, the carter's horse shifts in its harness.
The lower flight is quiet. The candle streak on the wall has dried to nothing and the loose tread does not creak under an empty house.
Lavinia Netherby stands at the dog-leg turn with her box against her hip, waiting for you to pass. She does not speak. Her eyes go to the candle streak and away.

The fire is out and the fender cold. The reading lamp has been emptied, the tantalus locked, the tallow drip scraped from the writing table by someone who did not do it well. The inside lock gleams where the Major's man oiled it for his notes.

Mr Yardley waits at the end window with his back to the study door, looking down at the drive. The master's bell hangs still on its wire. The bare boards show where the fire bucket stood for two days and stands no longer.

actions.label: 'What will stand, sir?'
actions.text: He does not look up from the Major's pocket. 'Your rounds book stands. The stub stands with it. The key stands if the Major says where it was found and you say when.' He closes the Major's coat over it himself. 'The rest is a house talking, and houses are not sworn.'

actions.label: 'The carter is waiting, Mr Fairbrother.'
actions.text: He takes up his box as if it weighed nothing, which after forty years it does. Lavinia comes down the last flight behind him without a word and the two boxes are roped on the cart's tail together. What he says to the carter, you do not hear; the baize door swings shut on it. The back stairs are quiet.

actions.detail: 'The key, sir. Is it to be kept locked?'
actions.label: 'Is it to be kept locked, sir?'
actions.text: He does not turn from the window. 'Locked. Until the spring, at least. I shan't use it.' A pause. 'You saw where everyone was. You'll have seen where I was.' He waits for you to answer and you do not, and he nods as if that were the answer.

actions.label: lock the study door
actions.text: The carriage is gone down the thawing drive and the cart after it. The new master's key turns in the lock with the small clean sound the old one made from the inside. You stand with it warm in your hand and an apron with nothing in it; the house is quieter by four people, and the master's name went down the drive with them.

events.text: Wheels grind on the gravel below. Major Carrington and Mr Ellingham are gone down the drive with what the house has decided, and the half-landing window shows only slush and two black ruts.

nudges.text: Somewhere below, the carter's horse stamps and the harness rings. The first cart will not wait on the house.
Mr Yardley's voice, carrying along the gallery: 'The study, when you have a moment. I should like it locked before dark.'

Cornelius Ellingham at his elbow with a folded paper, mouth half-open mid-sentence
far below through the stair well, the top of a servant's head and a cord-tied wooden box
frame.environment: Morning after the thaw; flat grey snow light through tall windows, meltwater streaking the glass, lamps unlit, cold air
frame.palette_mood: Grey, slate and wet black, a single warm brown of the wooden box; subdued, final, watchful
